vignette:
Moana is a 56-year-old married woman of Pacific Islander background who has spent much of her adult life in social ministry work, the kind of person who had long defined herself by her steadiness with people in crisis, her ability to sit with suffering without losing her footing. The assault happened in a context that made that confidence feel especially shattered to her. She had been with people she knew, related to others in her community, in an ordinary setting that had not seemed dangerous. Because the man was not a stranger, but someone connected to familiar people, the violation landed in a way that altered how she moved through her world afterward. What stayed with her was not only the sexual assault itself but the unbearable clarity of certain moments: the room, the feeling in her body, the sense of suddenly being trapped in a situation she had not imagined could happen there. When she speaks about it now, the memory arrives with cinematic force, as if a scene starts running in front of her without her permission. She does not describe it as vague or dreamlike. On the contrary, it is painfully detailed, too clear, the kind of replay that seizes her in the middle of other things.

In the weeks after, Moana found that contact with people linked, even loosely, to the perpetrator or to that circle of acquaintances could set something off in her immediately. A familiar surname, seeing a related family member at church or in the community, even anticipating that she might cross paths with “those people,” could make her body tighten before she had time to think. She became superalert in ways she had never been before. She scanned rooms automatically, noticed exits first, and chose her seat based on how quickly she could leave. At work, where she met parishioners and families in offices and community rooms, she began positioning herself nearest the door no matter how awkward it looked. She felt embarrassed by how deliberate it was, but the alternative felt impossible. Her body stayed tense, braced, as if danger might break through at any moment. At night she checked doors and windows repeatedly, then checked them again. She knew, on one level, that the locks were already set, but she could not settle until she had verified them herself.

What troubled her almost as much as the fear was the way ordinary moments of ease seemed to become dangerous. If she noticed herself relaxing with her husband, laughing, or feeling briefly happy, she would suddenly stiffen. Feeling good no longer registered as simple relief; it made her uneasy, as though letting her guard down invited something terrible. She began to mistrust her own comfort. Even a vague sense of discomfort in her body or surroundings could start the internal replay. The memory would force itself in, unbidden, while she was driving, cooking, or preparing for a meeting, and suddenly she was back inside those images again.

Over the following months, she developed habits that made sense to her in the moment. She wore heavy make-up with unusual care, treating her face almost like armor before leaving the house. She ate excessively when the tension built, especially after difficult encounters or after seeing someone who reminded her of the network around the assault. The eating gave her something immediate to do with the agitation, though afterward she often felt ashamed and flat. These changes were visible enough that they affected how she experienced herself in her role. She had once thought of herself as capable, composed, and deeply present with others. Now she had come to believe there was something wrong with her as a person. She told herself that somebody else would have stopped what happened, that another woman would have seen it sooner, pushed back harder, gotten out. From there it was a short step in her mind to a harsher conclusion: that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her for decades.

That belief began to reach into her marriage and work. Her husband saw the repeated lock-checking and the restlessness in her body at night. At work, she was still turning up and performing her duties, but with a narrower range of ease. She noticed herself planning every visit around exits and watching people more than she listened to them. In community settings where she once moved freely, she kept alert for related people and silently calculated how to avoid being cornered. She experienced this not as caution but as evidence that she had changed in some essential way.

By the time she sought help, the accumulation of these patterns had become impossible for her to dismiss. What finally brought her in was not one single crisis, but the recognition that she was living as if under constant threat and that even happiness no longer felt safe. She wants relief from the relentless replay of the assault and from the exhausting watchfulness that follows her through home, ministry, and community life. What frightens her most is the possibility that the assault has revealed something defective in her and that the capable woman she once knew herself to be is gone for good. What she hopes, more quietly, is that she might still find a way to feel at ease in her own body and among her own people again.
